query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an HVOF-deposited oxide coating to a titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy will improve its mechanical performance under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment conditions compared to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy where Ti and Ni are primary constituents.
generation.intervention: Use high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) deposition to form an adherent, fine-grained oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., ≥800 °C) or in extreme environments with high oxidizing atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a compact, fine-grained oxide scale that adheres strongly to the alloy surface, reducing oxidation penetration and providing surface reinforcement.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating/cooling rates in HVOF deposition create a non-equilibrium oxide layer with refined grains, which acts both as a barrier against high-temperature oxidation and as a reinforcement that limits surface microstructural degradation, leading to enhanced hardness and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated Ti–Ni HEA will exhibit higher hardness, improved yield/compressive strength, and better oxidation resistance than the same material without the coating when subjected to high-temperature or aggressive environmental exposures.
generation.baseline: The uncoated Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy tested under the same elevated-temperature/extreme-environment conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Ti–Ni HEAs in a single-phase solid-solution state within the composition range where Ti and Ni are primary constituents, and the test regime should include temperatures around or above 800 °C and/or similarly severe environmental conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the performance improvement and the optimal oxide layer thickness/structure remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Ti–Ni HEA samples. Apply an HVOF-deposited oxide coating to one set while leaving the other uncoated. Subject both sets to accelerated high-temperature and oxidative environments (e.g., exposure to 800–1100 °C and oxidizing atmospheres) over a fixed duration. Perform mechanical tests (microhardness, yield/compressive strength) and oxidation resistance assessments (weight gain measurements, oxide scale integrity via SEM/EDS) on both sets.
measurements: Microhardness and tensile/compressive strength at elevated temperatures
Oxidation weight gain and oxide scale thickness/integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If statistical analysis shows that the coated samples do not exhibit a significant improvement (beyond experimental variance) in mechanical properties or oxidation resistance compared to the uncoated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application. reading.lever: Use HVOF deposition to form an adherent, fine-grained oxide layer that protects and reinforces the Ti–Ni HEA at high temperatures.
reading.why: Prior HVOF studies on related HEAs demonstrated enhanced high-temperature hardness and oxidation resistance, making this approach promising for the Ti–Ni system.
